idiom_name: role state as enum/typestate, or TypeId-keyed extension map (classic role objects are not idiomatic)
implementation_notes: Rust has no inheritance and no implicit conformance between unrelated trait objects, so a role object cannot be usable wherever the core is, which is the half of the pattern that makes its views transparent. The other half - a core that owns roles while each role refers back to that core - is a reference cycle that needs Rc<RefCell<..>> plus Weak or an arena, and the standard library documents that &dyn Any can only test concrete types and cannot test whether a type implements a trait. Idiomatic Rust therefore models roles as data: an enum or typestate dispatched with match for closed role sets, explicit trait-object composition for sets fixed at construction, or a TypeId-keyed extension map when dynamic extensibility is genuinely required. Emulate the classic structure only when mirroring an external model whose roles really are runtime-attached objects - and expect explicit downcasts and hand-managed lifetimes.
pitfalls: TypeId requires 'static and identifies concrete types only: downcast_ref cannot ask whether a stored role implements a trait, and type_id() on a Box<dyn Any> returns the container's id, not the value's.
Rc<RefCell<Core>> cycles between core and roles leak and turn borrow mistakes into runtime panics; prefer Weak references, arenas or indices.
Storing roles as Send + Sync trait objects infects the core's API with bounds and is easy to get wrong under async executors.
alternative: Model the role set explicitly: an enum of role states dispatched with match (or typestate when transitions are compile-time known) for closed role sets, an explicit composition of trait objects when the set is fixed at construction, or a TypeId-keyed extension map (TypeId -> Box<dyn Any>) when dynamic extensibility is genuinely required.
